trap.title: The office, not the person
trap.body: Tossups on this office are packed with famous holders, such as Thomas Jefferson, William Seward, George Marshall, and Henry Kissinger, so it is tempting to buzz with a name; that is wrong when the question asks for “this office” or “this cabinet post.” Players also mix it up with other cabinet jobs: Alexander Hamilton was Secretary of the Treasury, and the Secretary of War ran the Army until 1947. The department this official runs, the State Department, is a separate answer line.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This office,” “this post,” or “this position” wants the Secretary of State; “this department” wants the State Department; “this man” or “this woman” wants a person. Treaties, embassies, and diplomats point here, not to Defense or the Treasury.
trap.line: Real answer line: Secretary of State (prompt on Secretary or State Department; do not accept other cabinet posts or “Vice President”)

topics.name: Tecumseh
topics.kicker: Shawnee leader of a Native confederacy · British ally in the War of 1812
topics.briefing: Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who believed that Native lands belonged to all Native peoples together, so no single nation had the right to sell them. With his younger brother Tenskwatawa, called “the Prophet,” he built a confederacy of many nations to stop American settlers from pushing farther west. He fought alongside the British in the War of 1812 and was killed at the Battle of the Thames in 1813, in what is now Ontario.
topics.answerHtml: Tecumseh (accept Tecumtha; do not accept “Tenskwatawa” or “William Tecumseh Sherman”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Midshipmen at the U.S. Naval Academy toss pennies for luck at a bronze statue nicknamed for this man, and they paint it before big football games. The ship figurehead that the statue copies was actually meant to show the Delaware leader Tamanend.
tossups.r: A Union general who marched through Georgia had this man’s name as his middle name. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who allied with the British in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: Supporters of Richard Mentor Johnson, who later became Martin Van Buren’s vice president, used a campaign rhyme claiming that Johnson had killed this man. This man died in October 1813 at a battle near Moraviantown, and his body was never positively identified.
tossups.r: That battle was the Battle of the Thames [“TEMZ”]. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who fought for the British in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: This man’s father was killed at the Battle of Point Pleasant in 1774. Twenty years later, this man fought against “Mad Anthony” Wayne’s army at the Battle of Fallen Timbers, and he refused to sign the Treaty of Greenville that followed.
tossups.r: He later built a confederacy of Native nations. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader whose brother Tenskwatawa [“ten-SKWAH-tuh-wah”] was called “the Prophet.”

tossups.p: In 1810, this man told a territorial governor at Vincennes [“vin-SENZ”] that the Treaty of Fort Wayne was invalid, arguing that no single nation could sell land that belonged to all Native peoples in common. He met that governor there again in 1811 before traveling south to seek allies.
tossups.r: That governor, William Henry Harrison, then won the Battle of Tippecanoe while this man was away. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader.

tossups.p: In 1805, this man’s younger brother, then called Lalawethika, had a vision and began preaching that Native people should give up alcohol and American goods. In 1808, the two brothers founded a village where the Tippecanoe River meets the Wabash.
tossups.r: That village was called Prophetstown. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who built a confederacy of Native nations.

tossups.p: While this man was away recruiting allies in the South, warriors following his brother attacked William Henry Harrison’s camp before dawn in November 1811. Harrison’s troops held their ground, then burned the village where this man and his brother had gathered followers from many nations.
tossups.r: That battle was Tippecanoe. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader whose brother was called “the Prophet.”

tossups.p: In 1811, this man spoke at a great council in the Creek town of Tuckabatchee [“tuck-uh-BATCH-ee”], urging the Creeks to join a Native alliance. His visit inspired the Red Sticks, Creek warriors who were later defeated by Andrew Jackson at Horseshoe Bend in 1814.
tossups.r: His brother was Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet.” For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who allied with Britain in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: The British general Isaac Brock praised this man’s courage and skill before Brock was killed at Queenston Heights in October 1812. Two months earlier, this man and Brock had forced the American commander William Hull to surrender Detroit without a battle.
tossups.r: This man was killed the next year at the Battle of the Thames. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who fought for the British in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: After a battle near Fort Meigs in 1813, this man stopped warriors from attacking American prisoners. Later that year, after the British lost control of Lake Erie, he urged the British commander, Henry Procter, to stop retreating and fight.
tossups.r: That stand came at the Battle of the Thames, where this man was killed. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader.

tossups.p: This man’s name is often translated as “Shooting Star” or “Panther Across the Sky.” According to legend, he predicted the New Madrid earthquakes that shook the Mississippi Valley in the winter of 1811 to 1812. He was born around 1768 in what is now Ohio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader whose brother, Tenskwatawa, was known as “the Prophet.”

tossups.p: A territorial governor who opposed this man called him “one of those uncommon geniuses” who “spring up occasionally to produce revolutions.” This man traveled hundreds of miles, from the Great Lakes to the Creek towns of the South, trying to unite Native nations against American expansion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who was killed at the Battle of the Thames in 1813.

tossups.p: After the governor of Indiana Territory dared this man’s brother to prove his spiritual powers, the brother correctly predicted a total solar eclipse in June 1806. This man used his brother’s growing fame to help build a confederacy of Native nations.
tossups.r: That brother was Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet.” For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who died in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: At the peace talks in Ghent in 1814, British diplomats at first demanded a Native buffer state in the Great Lakes region, a homeland like the one this man had fought for, but they dropped the idea. This man had died fighting beside British troops the year before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader who was killed at the Battle of the Thames.

tossups.p: In the battle where this man died, the British line broke almost at once, but his warriors kept fighting from a swampy thicket against Kentucky mounted riflemen. The British general Henry Procter fled the field and was later court-martialed.
tossups.r: That battle was the Battle of the Thames in 1813. For 10 points, name this Shawnee ally of Britain in the War of 1812.

tossups.p: The Shawnee chief Black Hoof, who favored peaceful farming at Wapakoneta [“wah-puh-kuh-NET-uh”], refused to join this man’s movement. This man and his brother instead drew followers from many nations, including the Potawatomi, Kickapoo, and Ho-Chunk, to their village on the Wabash River.
tossups.r: That village was Prophetstown. For 10 points, name this Shawnee leader whose brother was Tenskwatawa.

trap.title: Not Sherman, not the Prophet
trap.body: Three names collide here. Tecumseh was the Shawnee war leader who built the confederacy and died at the Thames in 1813; his younger brother Tenskwatawa, “the Prophet,” was the religious leader whose followers lost at Tippecanoe in 1811; and William Tecumseh Sherman was a Union general in the Civil War who was named after him. Answering “Tecumseh” on a Sherman question, or “Tenskwatawa” on a Tecumseh question, loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Visions, the 1806 solar eclipse, or giving up alcohol and American goods point to Tenskwatawa; the confederacy, the British alliance, Isaac Brock, or the Thames point to Tecumseh. Civil War clues like the March to the Sea or the capture of Atlanta mean Sherman.
trap.line: Real answer line: Tecumseh (accept Tecumtha; do not accept “Tenskwatawa” or “William Tecumseh Sherman”)

topics.name: Underground Railroad
topics.kicker: Secret network that helped enslaved people escape · Routes north to freedom
topics.briefing: The Underground Railroad was not underground and not a railroad: it was a secret network of people who helped enslaved people escape to the free states and Canada before the Civil War. Free Black people, white abolitionists, and many Quakers used railroad code words, calling guides “conductors” and safe houses “stations.” Harriet Tubman became its most famous conductor, and William Still of Philadelphia recorded the stories of hundreds of freedom seekers.
topics.answerHtml: Underground Railroad (prompt on Railroad; do not accept “Harriet Tubman”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1849, a man in Richmond, Virginia, had himself shipped in a wooden crate to abolitionists in Philadelphia, a trip that took more than a day. When the crate was opened, he climbed out and sang a hymn, and he became famous by the nickname “Box.”
tossups.r: Henry “Box” Brown escaped with help from this network. For 10 points, name this secret system of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people reach freedom.

tossups.p: While interviewing a formerly enslaved man in 1850, a Philadelphia clerk discovered that the man, Peter, was his own long-lost older brother. That clerk kept careful records of hundreds of people who passed through Philadelphia and published them in an 1872 book.
tossups.r: That man, William Still, is called the “Father” of this network. For 10 points, name this secret system that helped enslaved people escape to the North and Canada.

tossups.p: In Cincinnati, a Quaker merchant ran a store that sold only goods made without the labor of enslaved people. Earlier, he and his wife, Catharine, had sheltered so many freedom seekers at their home in Newport, Indiana, that he was nicknamed this network’s “President.”
tossups.r: That man was Levi Coffin. For 10 points, name this secret network that led enslaved people to freedom before the Civil War.

tossups.p: Under a law passed as part of the Compromise of 1850, federal commissioners earned ten dollars for sending an accused person back to slavery but only five dollars for setting the person free. After that law passed, many people helped by this network kept going all the way to Canada.
tossups.r: That law was the Fugitive Slave Act. For 10 points, name this secret network of routes and safe houses, whose most famous conductor was Harriet Tubman.

tossups.p: In 1848, Ellen Craft disguised herself as a sickly young white man with her arm in a sling, so no one would ask her to write, while her husband, William, pretended to be her servant. The couple traveled openly by train and steamboat from Macon, Georgia, to Philadelphia.
tossups.r: Abolitionists there and in Boston helped them through this network. For 10 points, name this secret system of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape.

tossups.p: A Presbyterian minister named John Rankin kept a lantern burning in his hilltop house in Ripley, Ohio, as a signal to people crossing the Ohio River to freedom. A story Harriet Beecher Stowe heard about a woman crossing that river on the ice inspired the character Eliza in _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_.
tossups.r: Rankin’s home was a “station” on this network. For 10 points, name this secret system that helped enslaved people escape to the North.

tossups.p: In 1858, students and teachers from Oberlin, Ohio, rescued a man named John Price from slave catchers in the nearby town of Wellington and hid him until he could reach Canada. Oberlin College, one of the first colleges to admit Black students, was a busy center of this network.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret network of routes and safe houses that helped people escape slavery.

tossups.p: A Quaker in Wilmington, Delaware, who helped thousands of people escape slavery, was fined so heavily by a federal court in 1848 that he lost almost everything. He reportedly told the courtroom that anyone who knew a freedom seeker needing shelter should send that person to him.
tossups.r: That man, Thomas Garrett, often sheltered Harriet Tubman. For 10 points, name this secret network of “conductors” and “stations.”

tossups.p: Josiah Henson, who had escaped from slavery in Kentucky, helped found the Dawn Settlement in what is now Ontario, a community for people who reached Canada through this network. Henson’s life story is often said to have inspired the title character of _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret network that helped enslaved people escape to the North and Canada.

tossups.p: The National Park Service runs a “Network to Freedom” program that recognizes historic sites of this network, and a national museum about it opened in 2004 on the banks of the Ohio River in Cincinnati. Crossing that river meant leaving the slave state of Kentucky for the free state of Ohio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret system of routes and safe houses whose “conductors” guided people to freedom.

tossups.p: Because Britain had ended slavery throughout its empire in 1834, many people helped by this network settled in Canadian towns such as St. Catharines and Chatham. People who hid freedom seekers along the way were called “stationmasters,” and those who donated money were called “stockholders.”
tossups.r: Guides like Harriet Tubman were called “conductors.” For 10 points, name this secret network that helped enslaved people escape before the Civil War.

tossups.p: After escaping slavery in 1838, a famous abolitionist hid freedom seekers at his home in Rochester, New York, as part of this network, helping them cross Lake Ontario to Canada. He named his newspaper _The North Star_ after the star that guided many people escaping north.
tossups.r: That man was Frederick Douglass. For 10 points, name this network of secret routes whose “stations” were safe houses.

tossups.p: Some guides on this network started escapes on Saturday nights, because reward notices for runaways could not appear in the newspapers until Monday. Freedom seekers often traveled at night, following the North Star, which the Big Dipper, sometimes called the “drinking gourd,” points toward.
tossups.r: Its most famous conductor, Harriet Tubman, said she “never lost a passenger.” For 10 points, name this secret network that helped enslaved people escape.

tossups.p: According to one story, a man named Tice Davids swam across the Ohio River from Kentucky in 1831 and vanished so completely that his enslaver gave this network its name. Ripley, Ohio, where Davids landed, became one of the busiest crossing points on the river.
tossups.r: The enslaver said Davids must have escaped on an “underground road.” For 10 points, name this secret network of routes and safe houses.

tossups.p: In _Prigg v. Pennsylvania_, the Supreme Court ruled in 1842 that states did not have to help enforce the federal law on escaped enslaved people. Many Northern states then passed “personal liberty laws” that made it harder to capture people who escaped through this network.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this secret network of routes, safe houses, and “conductors” that helped enslaved people reach freedom.

clues.t: A secret network of people, routes, and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape to the free states and Canada before the Civil War
Harriet Tubman was its most famous “conductor”; she said she “never lost a passenger”
Used train code words: guides were “conductors” and safe houses were “stations”
Freedom seekers often traveled at night, following the North Star
Helpers included free Black people, white abolitionists, and many Quakers
William Still of Philadelphia, its “Father,” recorded hundreds of escapes and found his long-lost brother Peter in 1850
Quaker Levi Coffin, its “President,” sheltered freedom seekers in Newport, Indiana, and later in Cincinnati
The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made Northerners help catch people who escaped, so many freedom seekers went on to Canada
Henry “Box” Brown had himself shipped in a wooden crate from Richmond to Philadelphia (1849)
William and Ellen Craft escaped in 1848, with Ellen disguised as a sickly young white man and William as her servant
John Rankin’s hilltop house in Ripley, Ohio, signaled people crossing the Ohio River; a story of a crossing on the ice inspired Eliza in _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_
Quaker Thomas Garrett of Wilmington, Delaware, kept helping after a huge federal fine in 1848; he often sheltered Harriet Tubman
Levi Coffin ran a Cincinnati store that sold only goods made without enslaved labor
Under the 1850 law, commissioners got $10 for returning a person to slavery but only $5 for setting the person free
Oberlin–Wellington Rescue (1858): people from Oberlin, Ohio, freed John Price; Oberlin College was one of the first to admit Black students
Josiah Henson helped found the Dawn Settlement in Ontario; his life story is often linked to _Uncle Tom’s Cabin_
A national museum about it opened in Cincinnati in 2004; the National Park Service runs a “Network to Freedom” program
Britain ended slavery in its empire in 1834, so Canadian towns like St. Catharines and Chatham became new homes
Donors were “stockholders,” hosts were “stationmasters,” and the people helped were “passengers” or “cargo”
Frederick Douglass hid freedom seekers at his home in Rochester, New York, near the Lake Ontario crossing to Canada
Some guides began escapes on Saturday nights, since reward notices could not run in newspapers until Monday
The Big Dipper, sometimes called the “drinking gourd,” points toward the North Star
One story says it got its name after Tice Davids crossed the Ohio River to Ripley in 1831 and seemed to vanish
_Prigg v. Pennsylvania_ (1842) and Northern “personal liberty laws” made capturing escapees harder, until the stricter 1850 law

trap.title: Network, conductor, or law?
trap.body: Underground Railroad tossups are full of people and laws that are answers of their own. Harriet Tubman was its most famous conductor, William Still and Levi Coffin were leaders, and the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 made the work far more dangerous, so a question asking for “this woman,” “this man,” or “this law” wants one of those instead.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this network,” “this system,” or “this organization” wants the Underground Railroad; “this woman” or “this conductor” wants Harriet Tubman; “this law” wants the Fugitive Slave Act. Saying only “railroad” earns a prompt, and the First Transcontinental Railroad is a completely different answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Underground Railroad (prompt on Railroad; do not accept “Harriet Tubman”)

topics.name: Washington, D.C.
topics.kicker: Capital of the United States since 1800 · Federal district on the Potomac
topics.briefing: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States, but it is not part of any state. The Residence Act of 1790 put the capital on the Potomac River, George Washington picked the exact spot, and Pierre L’Enfant designed a city of wide avenues, while Benjamin Banneker helped survey its borders. The government moved there in 1800, and British troops burned the Capitol and the White House during the War of 1812.
topics.answerHtml: Washington, D.C. (accept District of Columbia or D.C.; do not accept “Washington State” or “George Washington”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Residence Act of 1790 called for building this city along the Potomac River. Its location came out of a deal made at a dinner hosted by Thomas Jefferson, in which Alexander Hamilton won Southern votes for his plan to take over the states’ war debts.
tossups.r: Philadelphia served as the temporary capital until the government moved here in 1800. For 10 points, name this capital city of the United States.

tossups.p: A French-born engineer who had fought in the Continental Army drew this city’s plan of wide avenues cutting diagonally across a grid, but he was fired in 1792 after clashing with officials. In 1909, his remains were reburied at Arlington National Cemetery on a hill overlooking this city.
tossups.r: That engineer was Pierre L’Enfant [“lahn-FAHN”]. For 10 points, name this capital city on the Potomac River.

tossups.p: A self-taught astronomer who later sent Thomas Jefferson a copy of his almanac, along with a letter challenging Jefferson’s views on race, helped Andrew Ellicott survey this city’s borders in 1791. Many of the boundary stones from that survey, set about a mile apart, still stand.
tossups.r: That man was Benjamin Banneker. For 10 points, name this federal city laid out on land from Maryland and Virginia.

tossups.p: A day after enemy troops set fire to this city, a violent storm that included a tornado swept through it and helped put out the flames. Those troops had marched in after routing American militia at Bladensburg, Maryland, in August 1814.
tossups.r: Dolley Madison had a famous portrait of the first president saved before the White House burned. For 10 points, name this city that British troops burned during the War of 1812.

tossups.p: Residents of this city first voted for president in 1964. A 1961 amendment gave this city electoral votes, but no more than the least populous state has, so it has three. Its delegate in the House cannot vote on final passage of bills.
tossups.r: That amendment was the 23rd. For 10 points, name this federal district, the capital of the United States.

tossups.p: A British scientist who never visited the United States left his fortune to found an institution of learning in this city, and in 1904 Alexander Graham Bell brought that scientist’s remains here from Italy. That institution’s red sandstone “Castle” stands on the National Mall.
tossups.r: That institution is the Smithsonian. For 10 points, name this capital city, home to the National Air and Space Museum.

tossups.p: In 1846, Congress gave back to Virginia the part of this capital’s original ten-mile square that lay across the Potomac, including the port of Alexandria. That land includes Arlington, where the Pentagon and Arlington National Cemetery were later built.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal district that originally took land from both Virginia and Maryland.

tossups.p: Every April 16, this city celebrates Emancipation Day, marking an 1862 law that freed enslaved people here about nine months before the Emancipation Proclamation. That law paid slaveholders who were loyal to the Union for each person freed.
tossups.r: The Compromise of 1850 had already banned the slave trade, but not slavery, here. For 10 points, name this capital city.

tossups.p: Many license plates in this city carry a protest slogan about “taxation without representation,” because its residents pay federal taxes but have no voting member of Congress. The Home Rule Act of 1973 allowed its residents to elect a mayor and a council.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal district, the capital of the United States, which is not part of any state.

tossups.p: In 1912, the mayor of Tokyo, Yukio Ozaki, sent about three thousand cherry trees to this city, and First Lady Helen Taft planted one of the first two near the Tidal Basin. Each spring, a festival celebrates the blooming of those trees.
tossups.r: Many of those trees stand near the Jefferson Memorial. For 10 points, name this U.S. capital, also home to the Lincoln Memorial.

tossups.p: Construction of an obelisk honoring the first president stopped for more than twenty years, so its marble changes color partway up. When it was finished in 1884, that obelisk in this city was the tallest structure in the world.
tossups.r: It stands on the National Mall between the Capitol and the Lincoln Memorial. For 10 points, name this capital city.

tossups.p: Article One of the Constitution lets Congress rule a district “not exceeding ten miles square” as the seat of government. Thomas Jefferson’s 1801 inauguration was the first held in this city, and John Adams was the first president to live here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital city of the United States, which is not part of any state.

tossups.p: An 1871 law merged this city with Georgetown into a single territorial government, and Alexander “Boss” Shepherd then paved streets and built sewers so quickly that the government ran up huge debts. Congress ended that territorial government in 1874.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this capital city on the Potomac River, whose government Congress controls.

tossups.p: Frederick Douglass spent his last years at Cedar Hill, a house in this city’s Anacostia neighborhood. Bills to make most of this city a state named partly for Douglass passed the House of Representatives in 2020 and 2021 but did not pass the Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this federal district, which has three electoral votes under the 23rd Amendment.

tossups.p: After the Library of Congress burned in 1814, Thomas Jefferson sold his collection of more than six thousand books to restart it. The library’s oldest building, which is named for Jefferson, stands across the street from the Capitol in this city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city where Pennsylvania Avenue links the Capitol and the White House.

clues.t: Capital of the United States since 1800; a federal district that is not part of any state
Built on the Potomac River, on land that came from Maryland and Virginia
Home of the White House, the Capitol, the Lincoln Memorial, and the National Mall
Named for the first president, who chose its exact site
British troops burned the Capitol and the White House here in August 1814, during the War of 1812
The Residence Act of 1790 put the capital on the Potomac; Philadelphia was the temporary capital until 1800
French-born engineer Pierre L’Enfant designed its plan of wide diagonal avenues across a grid (1791)
Benjamin Banneker, a free Black astronomer, helped Andrew Ellicott survey its boundaries (1791)
The 23rd Amendment (1961) gave it three electoral votes; residents first voted for president in 1964
Home of the Smithsonian Institution, founded in 1846 with money left by British scientist James Smithson
Its location came from a dinner deal among Hamilton, Jefferson, and Madison: Southern votes for Hamilton’s debt plan (Compromise of 1790)
Its residents have no voting member of Congress, only a House delegate who cannot vote on final passage of bills
Thomas Jefferson’s 1801 inauguration was the first held here; John Adams was the first president to live here
British troops marched in after routing militia at Bladensburg, Maryland; a storm with a tornado struck the next day
L’Enfant was fired in 1792 and reburied at Arlington National Cemetery in 1909
Banneker later sent Jefferson his almanac with a letter challenging Jefferson’s views on race; many boundary stones from the survey survive
In 1846, Congress gave the land across the Potomac, including Alexandria and Arlington, back to Virginia (retrocession)
Emancipation Day (April 16) marks an 1862 law that freed enslaved people here about nine months before the Emancipation Proclamation
The Compromise of 1850 banned the slave trade, but not slavery, in the capital
The Home Rule Act of 1973 lets residents elect a mayor and council; license plates protest “taxation without representation”
Alexander Graham Bell brought James Smithson’s remains from Italy in 1904; the Smithsonian “Castle” is red sandstone
Tokyo mayor Yukio Ozaki sent about 3,000 cherry trees in 1912; Helen Taft planted one of the first near the Tidal Basin
Its obelisk to the first president changes color partway up because building stopped for over 20 years; finished in 1884, it was the world’s tallest structure
Article One of the Constitution lets Congress govern a district “not exceeding ten miles square”
An 1871 law merged it with Georgetown; Alexander “Boss” Shepherd’s spending led Congress to end the territorial government in 1874
Frederick Douglass lived at Cedar Hill in Anacostia; statehood bills naming a state partly for him passed the House in 2020 and 2021
Thomas Jefferson sold his books to restart the Library of Congress after the 1814 fire

trap.title: City, state, or president?
trap.body: Three different answer lines share this name: George Washington, Washington, D.C., and Washington State. Clues about the Potomac River, L’Enfant’s street plan, the Smithsonian, or the 23rd Amendment want the city; Seattle, Mount Rainier, or Olympia mean the state; and clues about the first president’s life mean George Washington. Arlington National Cemetery and the Pentagon are across the river in Virginia, not in the city.
trap.fix: Listen for “this city,” “this district,” or “this capital.” For the city, “Washington” alone is fine, but if you add anything, make it “D.C.” or “District of Columbia,” never “State.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Washington, D.C. (accept District of Columbia or D.C.; do not accept “Washington State” or “George Washington”)

topics.name: Whiskey Rebellion
topics.kicker: Frontier revolt against a federal whiskey tax · A test of the new government
topics.briefing: In 1791, Congress passed Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton’s tax on whiskey to help pay the national debt. Frontier farmers in western Pennsylvania, who turned their extra grain into whiskey and even used it as money, refused to pay and attacked tax collectors, and in 1794 thousands of rebels gathered near Pittsburgh. President George Washington called up about 13,000 militiamen, and the rebellion fell apart, showing that the new federal government could enforce its laws.
topics.answerHtml: Whiskey Rebellion (accept Whiskey Insurrection; prompt on Whiskey; do not accept “Shays’ Rebellion” or “Fries’s Rebellion”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In July 1794, a federal marshal, David Lenox, rode with tax inspector John Neville to serve legal papers on farmers who had not paid a tax. The next day, armed men surrounded Neville’s home, Bower Hill, and they later burned it.
tossups.r: Alexander Hamilton had proposed that tax. For 10 points, name this 1794 uprising in western Pennsylvania against a federal tax on liquor.

tossups.p: On August 1, 1794, about seven thousand armed men gathered at Braddock’s Field, the site of a British defeat decades earlier, and talked of attacking the nearby town of Pittsburgh. After town leaders welcomed them, they marched peacefully through Pittsburgh instead.
tossups.r: President George Washington soon called out the militia. For 10 points, name this revolt by frontier farmers against Alexander Hamilton’s tax on liquor.

tossups.p: At a meeting at Parkinson’s Ferry in August 1794, a young Swiss-born politician urged angry farmers to avoid violence. That politician, Albert Gallatin, later served as Treasury Secretary under Thomas Jefferson, whose party repealed the tax that caused this event.
tossups.r: George Washington sent nearly 13,000 militiamen to end it. For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt in western Pennsylvania against a tax on distilled spirits.

tossups.p: Before the president could call out the militia under a 1792 law, Supreme Court Justice James Wilson had to certify that the courts could not enforce the law in the western part of his state. That certification came in August 1794, during this event.
tossups.r: Nearly 13,000 militiamen then marched west. For 10 points, name this uprising against Alexander Hamilton’s tax on whiskey.

tossups.p: Virginia governor Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee, the father of Robert E. Lee, commanded the army sent to end this event. The president rode out with that army as far as Bedford, Pennsylvania, before returning to Philadelphia.
tossups.r: That president, George Washington, was joined by Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt against a federal tax on liquor.

tossups.p: Philip Wigle and John Mitchell were the only two men convicted of treason after this event, and both were sentenced to death, but the president pardoned them in 1795. Most of the other prisoners taken to Philadelphia for trial were never convicted.
tossups.r: That president was George Washington. For 10 points, name this 1794 uprising against Alexander Hamilton’s excise tax on whiskey.

tossups.p: Under the law that sparked this event, large distillers could pay a yearly flat fee, while small producers usually paid by the gallon, which made them pay more per gallon. People charged with breaking that law had to stand trial in federal court in faraway Philadelphia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this frontier revolt in western Pennsylvania against a 1791 tax on whiskey.

tossups.p: Rebels in this event signed threatening letters with the made-up name “Tom the Tinker,” and they warned that anyone who obeyed the tax law would have their stills wrecked. Like the protesters of the American Revolution, they also put up liberty poles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1794 uprising in western Pennsylvania, put down by militia that George Washington called up.

tossups.p: In a speech to Congress in November 1794, the president blamed this event partly on “self-created societies,” meaning the Democratic-Republican clubs that had sprung up across the country. James Madison and other critics objected to that attack on the clubs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt against a federal tax on liquor, which Washington’s army ended without a battle.

tossups.p: The tax behind this event was the first federal tax on a product made inside the United States. Thomas Jefferson’s supporters in Congress repealed it in 1802, along with other internal taxes passed by the Federalists.
tossups.r: Rebels had gathered at Braddock’s Field near Pittsburgh. For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt against Alexander Hamilton’s tax on distilled spirits.

tossups.p: Hugh Henry Brackenridge, a Pittsburgh lawyer and the author of the novel _Modern Chivalry_, tried to steer the rebels in this event away from violence and later wrote a book defending his own role.
tossups.r: Farmers there turned extra grain into whiskey, which was easier to carry over the mountains and was even used as money. For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt against a federal tax.

tossups.p: Peace commissioners offered amnesty to people in this event who signed a promise to obey the law, but too few signed. The president then sent militia from four states: Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland, and Virginia.
tossups.r: Unlike the earlier Shays’ Rebellion, this revolt ended when a national army marched in. For 10 points, name this 1794 uprising against a federal tax on whiskey.

tossups.p: David Bradford, a lawyer who became one of the most radical leaders of this event, fled down the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers to Spanish territory when federal troops approached. John Adams later pardoned him. Bradford had called the rebels to gather at Braddock’s Field.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt in western Pennsylvania against Alexander Hamilton’s liquor tax.

tossups.p: Frontier farmers in this event were already angry that Spain had closed the lower Mississippi River to American shipping, so they could not easily sell their crops. Instead, they turned extra grain into a product that was easier to carry over the mountains and even used it as money.
tossups.r: A tax on that product, whiskey, set off this event. For 10 points, name this 1794 revolt in western Pennsylvania.

tossups.p: Five years after this event, John Fries [“FREEZ”] led farmers in eastern Pennsylvania in a revolt against a federal tax on houses and land, and John Adams later pardoned him. This earlier revolt, in the western part of the state, was set off by a 1791 tax.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1794 uprising against Alexander Hamilton’s tax on whiskey, which George Washington’s militia ended.

President George Washington called up about 13,000 militiamen to end it
Showed that the new federal government under the Constitution could enforce its laws
Frontier farmers turned extra grain into liquor, which was easier to haul over the mountains and was even used as money
About 7,000 rebels gathered at Braddock’s Field near Pittsburgh (August 1, 1794)
Rebels burned Bower Hill, the home of tax inspector John Neville (July 1794)
Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee led the army after Washington rode out with it as far as Bedford, Pennsylvania

Unlike Shays’ Rebellion under the Articles of Confederation, it was ended by a national army under the Constitution
Thomas Jefferson’s supporters in Congress repealed the tax in 1802
Federal marshal David Lenox rode with John Neville to serve legal papers on farmers just before Bower Hill was attacked
Albert Gallatin urged farmers to avoid violence at Parkinson’s Ferry (August 1794); he was later Jefferson’s Treasury Secretary
Justice James Wilson certified that the courts could not enforce the law, letting the president call out militia under the Militia Act of 1792
Large distillers could pay a flat fee while small producers paid by the gallon; cases were tried in faraway Philadelphia
Rebels signed threatening letters “Tom the Tinker” and put up liberty poles
Washington blamed “self-created societies,” the Democratic-Republican clubs, in a November 1794 speech to Congress
It was the first federal tax on a product made inside the United States
Hugh Henry Brackenridge, author of _Modern Chivalry_, tried to steer the rebels away from violence

Peace commissioners offered amnesty for a promise to obey the law, but too few signed

Not to be confused with Fries’s Rebellion (1799), a later revolt in eastern Pennsylvania over a tax on houses and land

trap.title: Whiskey, Shays’, or Fries’s?
trap.body: Three early tax revolts get mixed up. Shays’ Rebellion (1786–1787) was led by Daniel Shays in Massachusetts under the Articles of Confederation; the Whiskey Rebellion (1791–1794) was in western Pennsylvania against Hamilton’s tax on liquor; and Fries’s Rebellion (1799) was in eastern Pennsylvania against a tax on houses and land, ending with a pardon from John Adams.
trap.fix: Massachusetts, Daniel Shays, and the Springfield arsenal mean Shays’; Pittsburgh, Braddock’s Field, stills, and Washington’s militia mean Whiskey; John Fries and John Adams mean Fries’s. The Whiskey Ring was a separate scandal under Ulysses S. Grant.
trap.line: Real answer line: Whiskey Rebellion (accept Whiskey Insurrection; do not accept “Shays’ Rebellion” or “Fries’s Rebellion”)
